extracted.intended_audience: general readers, photographers, photojournalists, advertisers, and policy-makers interested in ethics and practices of image editing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for altering photographs across domains (art, journalism, advertising, science, social media), describing when edits are acceptable, unethical, regulated, or disqualifying. Covers technical, ethical, legal, and disclosure-related criteria with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and intent of photograph manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Photograph manipulation or photograph alteration is the modification of an otherwise genuine photograph. Some photograph manipulations are considered to be skillful artwork, while others are considered to be unethical practices, especially when used to deceive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish edits made for artistic/creative reasons from edits made to mislead. Evaluate a manipulated image by considering the creator's intent (art, storytelling, persuasion, deception) and the effect on viewers' understanding of reality (e.g., propaganda, fraud). Examples: artistic darkroom techniques (Ansel Adams) vs. doctored political images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and non-deceptive editing in photojournalism (NPPA standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The National Press Photographers Association (NPPA) Code of Ethics promotes the accuracy of published images, advising that photographers 'do not manipulate images ... that can mislead viewers or misrepresent subjects'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For news/photojournalism, edits that mislead or change the factual content are prohibited; minor tonal/contrast adjustments may be acceptable if they don't alter the content. When composite or significant alterations occur, disclosure is required. Examples and consequences: National Geographic vertical crop controversy, Newsweek cover composite disclosed on page 3, photographers resigning after discovered manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contest and award rules regarding manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Photo contests and awards may prohibit certain manipulations and can disqualify entries if rules are violated (e.g., World Press Photo disqualified a series after checking RAW-files and finding an element had been removed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contests commonly require original RAW files and may explicitly forbid removal/addition of elements; failure to provide originals or finding undisclosed alterations can result in disqualification. Note reported statistic: up to 20% of World Press Photo penultimate round entries were disqualified for manipulation/post-processing rule violations (as of a cited date).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific image transformation: accuracy, documentation, and artifact handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Raw astronomical images are generated from non-visible wavelengths and require decisions for how to transform raw data into colorized pictures; 'Both scientific accuracy and visual appeal contribute to the decisions, for both enabling accurate analysis by scientists and providing visual interest for the public.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In scientific imaging, transformations (color mapping, stacking, contrast enhancement, artifact removal) must be documented and justified so they do not mislead scientific interpretation. Examples: James Webb and Hubble wavelength-to-color mappings, stacking images, stitching observations, removing artifacts — always balance visual appeal with fidelity and document processing choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical retouching of human subjects (advertising/fashion/portrait)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common transformations include smoothing skin texture, erasing scars/pimples, slimming the subject's body, erasing wrinkles, altering hair/teeth/eye color; these practices raise concerns that they may lead to unrealistic expectations and negative body image among the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or producing retouched images of people, consider harms to audience body image and the subject's consent; some publishers/brands adopt policies to limit retouching or to run at least one unaltered photo (e.g., Seventeen's commitment). Industry practices (including 'reverse retouching') and AMA positions opposing extreme digital alterations should inform ethical standards. Where possible, label retouched images or avoid manipulations that create impossible body ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising truthfulness, legal compliance, and mandatory labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments and regulators are starting to ban photos that are too airbrushed and edited; examples include the UK Advertising Standards Authority banning misleading ads, France passing a law requiring models to show a healthy BMI and requiring labeling of edited photos, and Norway requiring labeling of body manipulations in advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising imagery must comply with jurisdictional rules about misleading representation and may require disclosure/labels for edited images of bodies. Noncompliance can lead to fines or other penalties (examples: France — fines and possible jail sentence; Norway — fines for failure to label). Evaluate ads for adherence to local advertising codes and statutory requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure and transparency for social media filters and influencer content
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media apps (Snapchat, Instagram, TikTok) provide filters that alter appearance in real-time; influencers use filters to increase engagement and can present unrealistic imagery, exposing especially younger users to manipulated idealized images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content that uses beauty filters or substantial real-time edits should be treated as potentially deceptive to naive viewers; platform policies, influencer transparency norms, and legal labeling requirements (where applicable) should guide disclosure. Consider the psychological impact on audiences when assessing appropriateness of filter use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent and harm considerations for deepfakes and nonconsensual manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Deepfakes (images/videos generated with deep-learning techniques) can be created for entertainment or nefarious purposes such as spreading disinformation; deepfake pornography superimposing faces without consent has become prevalent and is criticized due to lack of consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate manipulations for consent of depicted persons and potential for harm (privacy invasion, reputational damage, sexual exploitation). Nonconsensual use is ethically objectionable and may be illegal; special scrutiny required for political/financial/malicious uses (disinformation, fraud).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing artistic manipulation from documentary misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Depending on the application and intent, some photograph manipulations are considered an art form because they involve creation of unique images, while others are considered unethical when they distort documentary truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating images, clearly categorize purpose: art/creative work may permissibly transform content, while documentary/journalistic works should preserve factual content or disclose transformation. Examples: creative photomontage and darkroom compositing vs. misleading documentary edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology and trademark guidance: avoid using 'Photoshop' as a verb
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms 'Photoshop', 'photoshopped' and 'photoshopping' are ubiquitous, but Adobe Inc. objects to misuse of their trademarked software name and the Free Software Foundation advises against using 'photoshop' as a verb because Adobe Photoshop is proprietary software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer neutral terms like 'image editing' or 'digital manipulation' in formal writing to avoid trademark misuse and imprecision. Be aware of advocacy around terminology (trademark owner objections, FSF guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political propaganda and censorship misuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Photo manipulation has been used to deceive or persuade viewers for political purposes (propaganda) and for censorship (e.g., Stalin had Trotsky retouched out of photographs; removal of Nikolai Yezhov in Soviet press photos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess images for political intent and historical examples of manipulation used to erase individuals or rewrite events. Manipulations intended to alter public perception of political facts are ethically problematic and undermine trust; they should be labeled, contested, or treated as suspect evidence.
